enonce_intro_markdown: A car, of mass $1400\ \mathrm{kg}$, moves with a steady speed of $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ on a straight rough road with its engine working at a constant rate of $36\ \mathrm{kW}$.
incertitudes: Question 6 (c) : le sujet n'imprime pas de valeur de g pour cette question (« Take g as 10 » figure seulement après les questions 3 et 4). Valeur retenue : g = 9,8 m s^-2 (consigne du lot), P = 17 056 W (17,1 kW) ; avec g = 10 on obtiendrait 16 832 W (16,8 kW), valeur donnée entre parenthèses dans le corrigé.
Question 6 (c) : « its acceleration is 3/7 m s^-2 » est lue comme une accélération vers le bas de la pente (la voiture accélère en descendant).

questions.enonce_markdown: Calculate the resistance $R$ to the motion of the car if the road is horizontal.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model.** The car moves at constant speed on a horizontal road: the resultant force along the road is zero, so the driving force $F$ of the engine equals the resistance $R$. Positive direction: the direction of motion.

Power $=$ driving force $\times$ speed:

$$P = Fv \;\Rightarrow\; F = \frac{36\,000}{20} = 1800\ \mathrm N$$

$F - R = 0$, so

**$R = 1800\ \mathrm N$.**
themes: motion of a vehicle with resistance

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $R$ is proportional to the square of the speed $v$ of the car, show that $R = \dfrac{9v^2}{2}$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Since $R$ is proportional to $v^2$, $R = kv^2$ for a constant $k$. From part (a), $R = 1800\ \mathrm N$ when $v = 20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$:

$$k = \frac{1800}{20^2} = \frac{1800}{400} = \frac92$$

**Therefore $R = \dfrac{9v^2}{2}$ (newtons, with $v$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$), as required.**
themes: motion of a vehicle with resistance

questions.enonce_markdown: When the car is descending a straight road inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, where $\sin\theta = \dfrac1{20}$, and the resistance to the motion of the car remains unchanged, the speed of the car is $16\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ when its acceleration is $\dfrac37\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Calculate the rate at which the engine is working.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model and diagram.** The car goes down the slope (positive direction: down the slope). Forces along the slope: driving force $F$ of the engine (down the slope), the component of the weight $mg\sin\theta$ (down the slope), the resistance $R$ (up the slope). The car is speeding up, so the acceleration $a = \tfrac37\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ is down the slope. Take $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (no value printed for this question).

**Resistance at $16\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$** (law of part (b), unchanged):

$$R = \tfrac92(16)^2 = \tfrac92(256) = 1152\ \mathrm N$$

**Equation of motion** ($F_{net} = ma$ down the slope):

$$F + mg\sin\theta - R = ma$$

$$F + 1400(9.8)\left(\tfrac1{20}\right) - 1152 = 1400\times\tfrac37$$

$$F + 686 - 1152 = 600 \;\Rightarrow\; F = 1066\ \mathrm N$$

**Rate of working of the engine:**

$$P = Fv = 1066\times 16 = 17\,056\ \mathrm W \approx 17.1\ \mathrm{kW}$$

**The engine is working at about $17.1\ \mathrm{kW}$ ($17\,056\ \mathrm W$).** (With $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ one would get $F = 1052\ \mathrm N$ and $P = 16\,832\ \mathrm W \approx 16.8\ \mathrm{kW}$.)
themes: motion of a vehicle with resistance
